fields.sections.1.exchanges.0.pro.words: Knechtle argues that runaway protections, capital punishment for kidnapping, and debt or wartime contexts constrain biblical servitude, making its regulation morally significant.
fields.sections.1.exchanges.0.pro.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle grounds the regulation case in provisions protecting runaways, punishing kidnappers, and addressing debt, then connects wartime captivity to divine judgment rather than presenting biblical servitude as unrestricted ownership. Principal limitation: His sweeping claim that most Old Testament slavery involved culpable war prisoners lacks representative textual support, while the prison analogy compresses imprisonment, debt service, and captivity despite their consequential differences. Live burden: To establish defensibility, he must explain why these restrictions authorize the broader institution and justify enslavement specifically, especially when collective guilt is asserted without demonstrating individual wrongdoing or answering coercive permanent status. Locked score: The fixed 71 recognizes direct engagement through relevant legal texts, yet appropriately withholds stronger credit because the central wartime justification remains under-evidenced, overgeneralized, and insufficiently calibrated to contested interpretations.
